sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Establishment & Mandate**: Appointed in **1912** (submitted report in **1915**, published post-WWI in **1917**), the Islington Commission investigated the methods of recruitment and the employment of **Indians** in higher civil services.
• **Context of Appointment**: Prompted by persistent Indian nationalist demands for a larger share in governance, growing backlogs in judicial and executive efficiency, and the racial inequalities entrenched in the **Aitchison Commission (1886)** framework.
• **Core Dilemma**: Balancing the imperial imperative of maintaining ultimate British control and European standards of administration with the rising political pressure for **Indianisation**.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Recommended that **25%** of the superior posts in the Indian Civil Service (ICS) should be filled by Indians, a proportion criticized by nationalists as utterly inadequate.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Recruited directly in London by the Secretary of State; handled topmost administrative and judicial control.
Maintained absolute British hegemony and premium European salary scales.
Target of intense nationalist criticism for exclusion of Indians.
Recruited locally in India; handled subordinate executive and judicial roles (e.g., Deputy Collectors).
Stifled career progression of talented Indians stuck below the 'covenanted' ceiling.
Managed specialized departments like Railways, Posts & Telegraphs, and Customs operating across British India.
Gradually opened up to technical Indian experts due to administrative necessity.
Important for understanding the diversification of colonial bureaucracy.

items.definition: The policy demand by Indian nationalists to replace British bureaucrats with qualified Indians in high-ranking civil service positions to reduce the drain of wealth and foster self-governance.

Historical division where the Covenanted Civil Service (later ICS) was exclusively European, bound by covenants to the East India Company/Crown, while Uncovenanted services were open to locals in lower rungs.
The crucial nationalist demand to hold ICS examinations simultaneously in London and India, which the Islington Commission rejected, sparking massive political backlash.

The subsequent public service commission that superseded Islington's inadequate reforms by recommending a faster 40:40 split (ICS direct recruitment) and the establishment of a Public Service Commission.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Imperial Hubs**: London (India Office, Secretary of State, primary recruitment center for the ICS).
• **Provincial Administrative Centers**: Presidency capitals (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) and major provincial headquarters where Provincial Civil Services operated under severe structural caps.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Extreme racial bias, exorbitant salaries paid out of Indian revenues ('Home Charges'), denial of simultaneous exams, and sluggish promotion avenues for Indians.
• **Policy Interventions**: Recommendations were quickly overtaken by the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919)** and the eventual establishment of the **Federal Public Service Commission** under the Government of India Act 1935.

items.title: Mnemonic for British Indian Public Service Commissions
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: **A-I-L** (Aitchison, Islington, Lee)
• **Decoded Meaning**: **A**itchison (1886) -> **I**slington (1912) -> **L**ee (1923).
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly locks chronological order of major colonial administrative commissions for matching or sequencing questions.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Islington = **'25% Indianisation & NO simultaneous exams'**. Memorize this pairing to instantly clear trick MCQs.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that the Islington Commission recommended holding simultaneous civil service examinations in India and London. This is FALSE. The Commission rejected simultaneous exams, arguing it would lower administrative standards, though it recommended increasing Indian representation to 25%.

Mains Value Addition: In answers dealing with administrative evolution, analyze how the Islington Commission's conservative recommendations exposed the limits of British colonial reform, directly radicalizing the Home Rule Movement and pushing nationalists to demand complete dominion status.

keyTakeaways: The Islington Commission (1912-1915) was formed to evaluate public services and the degree of Indianisation in British India.
It notoriously recommended a meager 25% quota for Indians in the ICS and rejected holding simultaneous examinations in India.
Its conservative report catalyzed nationalist anger, leading directly to the more progressive Lee Commission (1923) and structural changes in the Government of India Act 1919.
